lessons.gloss: the vowel sign ◌ೀ — the long i the corpus has been printing since chapter two

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: You say nīnu and nīvu every time you address somebody. The mark that makes that i long is the one you have never been shown.
It is a vowel sign — it cannot stand alone, it rides on a consonant and changes the vowel that consonant carries.
Set it beside the short one you have read since chapter four:
This is the most-used character in this book that nothing has taught. It is in the word for you, in the colour blue, and in the polite verb ending you use whenever you ask somebody how they are.
You already say these:
ನೀನು / ನೀವು nīnu / nīvu — you, familiar and respectful.
ನೀಲಿ nīli — blue.
ನೀವು ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ? nīvu hēgiddīrā? — how are you? — and the ending carries it twice.
Put your pen on ◌ೀ (ī) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

lessons.title: ◌ೈ (ai) — the sign for the vowel that moves
lessons.gloss: the vowel sign ◌ೈ — the riding form of the ಐ you can now write

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: A chapter ago you wrote ಐ, the letter for ai. Here is the same vowel when a consonant is carrying it.
It is a vowel sign — it cannot stand alone, it rides on a consonant and changes the vowel that consonant carries.

ಐ and ◌ೈ are one vowel with two jobs. The letter opens a word; the sign sits on a consonant inside one. You met the pair idea with every other vowel in this script, and this is the last of them to arrive.
ಕ plus ◌ೈ gives ಕೈ — kai, a hand.
You already say these:
ತಲೆ ಕೈ tale kai — head and hand.
ವೈದ್ಯ vaidya — a doctor.
ರೈತ raita — a farmer.
Put your pen on ◌ೈ (ai) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

lessons.title: ◌ೌ (au) — the mark in the third word you learned
lessons.gloss: the vowel sign ◌ೌ — the mark inside the word for yes

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ◌ೌ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say yes in Kannada. That word has carried today's mark since chapter one.
It is a vowel sign — it cannot stand alone, it rides on a consonant and changes the vowel that consonant carries.
ಹ plus ◌ೌ gives ಹೌ — the first syllable of haudu.
Like ai, this vowel moves while you say it: it starts low and slides toward u. Two sounds in one mark, which is what the romanization's two letters are showing.

Every vowel in this script has two forms — a letter for the front of a word, a sign for inside one. This one's letter form is the single independent vowel whose stroke order this project has no source for, so the chapter that taught you to write the vowel letters stopped one short. The sign is what a reader actually meets on these pages, and it is the form this book can hand over honestly.
You already say these:
ಹೌದು haudu — yes.
ಗೌರವ gaurava — respect.
ಸೌಜನ್ಯ saujanya — courtesy.
Put your pen on ◌ೌ (au) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

lessons.title: ಣ (ṇa) — the n with the tongue curled back
lessons.gloss: the single character ಣ — the curled n, in the word for an eye

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ಣ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say the word for an eye. There are two n-sounds in Kannada and that word has the one you have never been shown.
ಣ — ṇa.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not ṇ, it is ṇa.
Kannada keeps two different n letters apart on the page, and English marks neither.

utterances: letter: ನ. romanized: na. where the tongue goes: tip behind the teeth.
letter: ಣ. romanized: ṇa. where the tongue goes: curled back along the roof.

segments.text: You have read ನ since the first chapter. ಣ (ṇa) is the same sound made further back, with the tongue curled — the position you already use for ಟ and ಡ.
You already say these:
ಕಣ್ಣು kaṇṇu — an eye.
ಸಿಗೋಣ sigōṇa — let us meet, inside the farewell.
ಖಂಡಿತ khaṇḍita — certainly.
Put your pen on ಣ (ṇa) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

lessons.title: ಶ (śa) — the letter every greeting starts with
lessons.gloss: the single character ಶ — the second of Kannada's three s letters, and the one every greeting opens on

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ಶ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say good morning, good evening and good night. All three begin on today's character.
ಶ — śa.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not ś, it is śa.
Every time-of-day greeting in this book opens with ಶುಭ śubha, “auspicious” — and that word begins on ಶ (śa).
Kannada prints three separate s letters, and you have had only one of them. ಸ you met in chapter twelve; ಶ (śa) is here; ಷ (ṣa) is on the next page.
You already say these:
ಶುಭ ರಾತ್ರಿ śubha rātri — good night.
ಶುಭೋದಯ śubhōdaya — good morning.
ಶುಭ ಸಂಜೆ śubha sañje — good evening.
Put your pen on ಶ (śa) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

lessons.title: ಷ (ṣa) — the third s, and the last one
lessons.gloss: the single character ಷ — the third s letter, curled back like ಣ

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on, your eyes, for letter shapes on the page and your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ಷ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Before the new one: ಶ (śa), and ಸ from chapter twelve. Today's is the third and final s-shape.
ಷ — ṣa.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not ṣ, it is ṣa.
Now you have the whole set:

utterances: letter: ಸ. romanized: sa. where the tongue goes: tip behind the teeth.
letter: ಶ. romanized: śa. where the tongue goes: flat against the front of the roof.
letter: ಷ. romanized: ṣa. where the tongue goes: curled back along the roof.

segments.text: ಷ (ṣa) curls back in the same place as ಣ (ṇa). That is the one position this script keeps naming and English never marks, and you have now met it on an n and on an s.
Look at ಸಂತೋಷ: it opens on ಸ and closes on ಷ (ṣa). Until today you could read one end of that word and not the other.
You already say these:
ಸಂತೋಷ santōṣa — joy; and how you say you are pleased to meet somebody.
ಇಷ್ಟ iṣṭa — liking.
ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ kṣamisi — sorry, excuse me.
Put your pen on ಷ (ṣa) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

lessons.title: (ೀ ೈ ೌ ಣ (ṇa) ಶ (śa) ಷ (ṣa)) (chihnegaLu mattu sa-galu) — six characters, two ideas

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. segments.source: [PAUSE 3s]

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say you the respectful way, and say yes. Name the mark each of those words carries.
One — a vowel can be long, or it can move. Three signs, and none of them can stand on its own:

utterances: sign: ◌ೀ. sound: ī. met in: ನೀವು — you.
sign: ◌ೈ. sound: ai. met in: ಕೈ — a hand.
sign: ◌ೌ. sound: au. met in: ಹೌದು — yes.

segments.text: Two — the tongue can curl back, and Kannada writes that position where English marks nothing:

utterances: flat: ನ na. curled: ಣ ṇa.
flat: ಸ sa. curled: ಷ ṣa.

segments.text: ಶ śa is the third s — flat against the front of the roof. One set of three where English has a single letter, and the word ಸಂತೋಷ uses two of them, one at each end.
